ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.7 (first sentence; Duncker p. 440) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 2; ANL vol. 6 p. 329)
greek: Γεγένηταί τις ὀνόματι Νοητός, τῷ γένει Σμυρναῖος. Οὗτος εἰσηγήσατο αἵρεσιν ἐκ τῶν Ἡρακλείτου δογμάτων·
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: There has appeared one, Noetus by name, and by birth a native of Smyrna. This person introduced a heresy from the tenets of Heraclitus.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 329; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Noetus of Smyrna is presented as the origin of a heresy derived from Heraclitus.
limits: Hippolytus' own polemical genealogy; it places Noetus outside the Church's teaching and says nothing about Hippolytus' positive Trinitarian doctrine.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.7 (Epigonus and Cleomenes; Duncker p. 440) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 2; ANL vol. 6 p. 329)
greek: οὗ διάκονος καὶ μαθητὴς γίνεται Ἐπίγονός τις τοὔνομα, ὃς τῇ Ῥώμῃ ἐπιδημήσας ἐπέσπειρε τὴν ἄθεον γνώμην. Οὗ μαθητεύσας Κλεομένης, καὶ βίῳ καὶ τρόπῳ ἀλλότριος τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ἐκράτυνε τὸ δόγμα,
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Now a certain man called Epigonus becomes his minister and pupil, and this person during his sojourn at Rome disseminated his godless opinion. But Cleomenes, who had become his disciple, an alien both in way of life and habits from the Church, was wont to corroborate the (Noetian) doctrine.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 329; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Epigonus brought the doctrine to Rome; his pupil Cleomenes strengthened it.
limits: Greek 'οὗ' (or 'Οἱ'/'Ὁ') at the start of the second sentence is uncertain at 130 dpi; check the original. Hippolytus is the only source for this succession.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.7 (Zephyrinus; Duncker p. 440) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 2; ANL vol. 6 p. 329)
greek: κατ᾽ ἐκεῖνο καιροῦ Ζεφυρίνου διέπειν νομίζοντος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, ἀνδρὸς ἰδιώτου καὶ αἰσχροκερδοῦς
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: At that time, Zephyrinus imagines that he administers the affairs of the Church — an uninformed and shamefully corrupt man. And he, being persuaded by proffered gain, was accustomed to connive at those who were present for the purpose of becoming disciples of Cleomenes.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 329; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Hippolytus describes Zephyrinus as ignorant and venal and says he tolerated Noetian teachers in Rome.
limits: Partisan testimony from a rival of the Roman bishops; not neutral evidence for Zephyrinus' doctrine. Accent on 'Ζεφυρίνου' read from image.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.9 (Heraclitus list; Duncker p. 442) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 4; ANL vol. 6 p. 331)
greek: Ἡράκλειτος μὲν οὖν φησιν εἶναι τὸ πᾶν διαιρετὸν ἀδιαίρετον, γενητὸν ἀγένητον, θνητὸν ἀθάνατον, λόγον, αἰῶνα, πατέρα υἱόν, θεὸν δίκαιον.
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Heraclitus then says that the universe is one, divisible and indivisible; generated and ungenerated; mortal and immortal; reason, eternity; Father, Son, and justice, God.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 331; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Hippolytus lists 'Father, Son' among Heraclitus' paradoxes to argue that Noetus' terms are Heraclitean, not Christian.
limits: Polemical argument by assimilation; it does not show what Hippolytus himself meant by Father and Son. Hippolytus' own Trinitarian statements are elsewhere (C. Noet., Ref. 10.33).

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.10 (Noetian formula on Son/Father; Duncker p. 448 and 450) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 5; ANL vol. 6 p. 335)
greek: Ὅτι δὲ καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν υἱὸν εἶναι λέγει καὶ πατέρα οὐδεὶς ἀγνοεῖ. λέγει δὲ οὕτως· Ὅτε μὲν οὖν μὴ γεγένητο ὁ πατήρ, δικαίως πατὴρ προσηγόρευτο· ὅτε δὲ ηὐδόκησεν γένεσιν ὑπομεῖναι, γεννηθεὶς ὁ υἱὸς ἐγένετο αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ, οὐχ ἑτέρου.
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Now, that Noetus affirms that the Son and Father are the same, no one is ignorant. But he makes his statement thus: When indeed, then, the Father had not been born, He yet was justly styled Father; and when it pleased Him to undergo generation, having been begotten, He Himself became His own Son, not another's.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 335; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: The formula says the Father became Son by generation, the Son being himself and not another; this is the 'Son became Son' pattern Hippolytus attacks.
limits: Greek 'λέγει' has no explicit subject. The preceding sentence names Heraclitus ('the Obscure'), so the Greek is ambiguous. ANF renders Noetus; ANL brackets '[Noetus]' as the translator's insertion. Treat attribution as unresolved. This is the main text for the 'Son became Son at the incarnation' objection; do not present it as Hippolytus' own view.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.10 (Noetian doctrine of God; Duncker p. 448) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 5; ANL vol. 6 p. 335)
greek: ἕνα καὶ τὸν αὐτὸν θεὸν εἶναι πάντων δημιουργὸν καὶ πατέρα, εὐδοκήσαντα δὲ πεφηνέναι τοῖς ἀρχῇθεν δικαίοις ὄντα ἀόρατον· ὅτε μὲν γὰρ οὐχ ὁρᾶται ἦν ἀόρατος, [ὅτε δὲ ὁρᾶται ὁρατός,] ἀχώρητος δὲ ὅτε μὴ χωρεῖσθαι θέλει, χωρητὸς [δὲ] ὅτε χωρεῖται·
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: For they advance statements after this manner — that one and the same God is the Creator and Father of all things; and that when it pleased Him, He nevertheless appeared, (though invisible,) to just men of old. For when He is not seen He is invisible; and He is incomprehensible when He does not wish to be comprehended, but comprehensible when he is comprehended.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 335; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: The Noetian God is invisible or visible, incomprehensible or comprehensible, according to his will.
limits: Hippolytus' report of the opponents' view, not his own. Bracketed words are editorial supplements in the edition. Useful for the 'God visible and passible' objection that Trinitarian writers had to answer.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.10-11 (names by time; Son from virgin; Duncker p. 450) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 5 (end); ANL vol. 6 p. 336)
greek: Οὕτως γὰρ δοκεῖ μοναρχίαν συνιστᾶν, ὃν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ φάσκων ὑπάρχειν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν καλούμενον, οὐχ ἕτερον ἐξ ἑτέρου, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ, ὀνόματι μὲν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν καλούμενον κατὰ χρόνων τροπήν, ἕνα δὲ εἶναι τοῦτον τὸν φανέντα καὶ γένεσιν ἐκ παρθένου ὑπομείναντα
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Father and Son, so called, are one and the same (substance), not one individual produced from a different one, but Himself from Himself; and that He is styled by name Father and Son, according to vicissitude of times. But that He is one who has appeared (among us), both having submitted to generation from a virgin.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 336; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Father and Son are names for one subject according to 'changes of time'; the one who appeared was generated from a virgin.
limits: The phrase 'according to changes of time' is the core of the modalist reading that Hippolytus rejects in Ref. 9. ANF 'substance' is a translator's supply. The ANL page is read from the OCR page header.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.11 (Zephyrinus' creed; Duncker p. 450) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 6; ANL vol. 6 p. 337)
greek: Ἐγὼ οἶδα ἕνα θεὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν, καὶ πλὴν αὐτοῦ ἕτερον οὐδένα γενητὸν καὶ παθητόν
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Now Callistus brought forward Zephyrinus himself, and induced him publicly to avow the following sentiments: I know that there is one God, Jesus Christ; nor except Him do I know any other that is begotten and amenable to suffering.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 337; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Zephyrinus, as Callistus' protege, is said to have confessed Christ alone as the one God, the only begotten and passible one.
limits: Hippolytus' report of a public formula attributed to Zephyrinus; the sentence is cut between Duncker pp. 450 and 452. Not a direct Trinitarian statement, and the source is hostile.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.11 (Father did not die; Duncker p. 452) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 6; ANL vol. 6 p. 337)
greek: ποτὲ δὲ λέγων· Οὐχ ὁ πατὴρ ἀπέθανεν, ἀλλὰ ὁ υἱός·
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: And on another occasion, when he would make the following statement: The Father did not die, but the Son.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 337; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Zephyrinus is quoted as saying that the Son, not the Father, died.
limits: Quoted through Hippolytus; the formula can be read as anti-patripassian, but the text does not give the speaker's full doctrine. Hippolytus' own reply is not in this passage.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.11 (Callistus calls them ditheists; Duncker p. 452) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 6; ANL vol. 6 p. 337)
greek: ἡμᾶς δὲ οὔ, ἀπεκάλει ἡμᾶς διθέους, ἐξεμῶν παρὰ βίαν τὸν ἐνδομυχοῦντα αὐτῷ ἰόν.
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: ...but not us, he called us worshippers of two gods, disgorging, independent of compulsion, the venom lurking within him.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 337; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Callistus accused Hippolytus and his party of worshipping two gods (ditheism).
limits: This is the charge itself, not Hippolytus' answer. The word 'διθέους' recurs at Duncker p. 458 ('δίθεοί ἐστε'). English is a fragment of the ANF sentence (ANF ch. 6, 'called us worshippers of two gods').

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.7 (Hippolytus denies collusion; Duncker p. 440-441) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 2; ANL vol. 6 p. 330)
greek: ἡμῶν μηδέποτε συγχωρησάντων, ἀλλὰ πλειστάκις ἀντικαθεστώτων πρὸς αὐτοὺς καὶ διελεγξάντων καὶ ἄκοντας βιασαμένων τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὁμολογεῖν
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Never at any time, however, have we been guilty of collusion with them; but we have frequently offered them opposition, and have refuted them, and have forced them reluctantly to acknowledge the truth.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 330; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Hippolytus says he never colluded with Zephyrinus and Callistus and opposed them repeatedly.
limits: Hippolytus' own self-description; a partisan claim with no independent confirmation in this passage. Shows the rival-bishop background.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.11-12 (Callistus' doctrine; Duncker p. 458) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 7; ANL vol. 6 p. 342)
greek: λέγων τὸν λόγον αὐτὸν εἶναι υἱόν, αὐτὸν καὶ πατέρα ὀνόματι μὲν καλούμενον, ἓν δὲ ὂν τὸ πνεῦμα ἀδιαίρετον· οὐκ ἄλλο εἶναι πατέρα, ἄλλο δὲ υἱόν, ἓν δὲ καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπάρχειν·
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Callistus alleges that the Logos Himself is Son, and that Himself is Father; and that though denominated by a different title, yet that in reality He is one indivisible spirit. And he maintains that the Father is not one person and the Son another, but that they are one and the same.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 342; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Callistus' doctrine: the Logos is himself Son and Father, one indivisible Spirit, with no distinction of persons.
limits: Hippolytus' summary of Callistus. Greek 'ἀδιαίρετον' is hyphenated across the line break in the image; read as 'ἀδιαί-ρετον'. This is the formula the question asked about ('the Logos himself is Son, himself Father, one indivisible spirit'). It is a monarchian formula that Hippolytus rejects.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.12 (prosopon; Duncker p. 458) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 7; ANL vol. 6 p. 343)
greek: καὶ τοῦτο ἓν ὂν πρόσωπον μὴ δύνασθαι εἶναι δύο, καὶ οὕτως τὸν πατέρα συμπεπονθέναι τῷ υἱῷ·
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: [abridged, with '...' for omitted words] For the Father, who subsisted in the Son Himself, after He had taken unto Himself our flesh, raised it to the nature of Deity... so that Father and Son must be styled one God, and that this Person being one, cannot be two.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 343; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Callistus argues that one prosopon cannot be two, so Father and Son must be one subject, and the Father suffered with the Son.
limits: Key Greek term 'πρόσωπον' in a monarchian argument: here it means one subject, not 'person' in the later Trinitarian sense. Hippolytus' own use of 'prosopa' (two persons) is in C. Noet. 14, not in this passage.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.12 (patripassian formula; Duncker p. 458) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 7; ANL vol. 6 p. 343)
greek: οὐ γὰρ θέλει λέγειν τὸν πατέρα πεπονθέναι καὶ ἓν εἶναι πρόσωπον
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: And in this way Callistus contends that the Father suffered along with the Son; for he does not wish to assert that the Father suffered, and is one Person, being careful to avoid blasphemy against the Father.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 343; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Callistus avoids saying that the Father suffered, but still holds that the Father suffered along with the Son.
limits: Hippolytus' report; the 'συμπεπονθέναι' (suffered together) formula is the patripassian point. Hippolytus' attack is at 'Father suffered with the Son' and is ad hominem here.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.11 (Callistus and Sabellius; Duncker p. 450) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 6; ANL vol. 6 p. 337)
greek: καὶ τοῖς μὲν ἀλήθειαν [λέγων ὅμοια] φρονοῦσι ποτὲ κατ᾽ ἰδίαν τὰ ὅμοια φρονεῖν [λέγων] ἠπάτα, πάλιν δ᾽ αὖ τοῖς τὰ Σαβελλίου ὁμοίως,
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: And to those who entertained true opinions, he would in private allege that they held similar doctrines (with himself), and thus make them his dupes; while at another time he would act similarly towards those (who embraced) the tenets of Sabellius.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 337; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Callistus deceived both orthodox and Sabellian listeners by claiming to agree with each.
limits: Partisan account; the bracketed words are editorial supplements. It shows the Sabellian link that Hippolytus uses against Callistus.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.12 (Carpophorus and banking; Duncker p. 452) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 7; ANL vol. 6 p. 338)
greek: Οἰκέτης ἐτύγχανε Καρποφόρου τινὸς ἀνδρὸς πιστοῦ ὄντος ἐκ τῆς Καίσαρος οἰκίας. Τούτῳ ὁ Καρποφόρος, ἅτε δὴ ὡς πιστῷ, χρῆμα οὐκ ὀλίγον κατεπίστευσεν, ἐπαγγειλάμενος κέρδος προσοίσειν ἐκ πραγματείας τραπεζιτικῆς·
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: Callistus happened to be a domestic of one Carpophorus, a man of the faith belonging to the household of Caesar. To this Callistus, as being of the faith, Carpophorus committed no inconsiderable amount of money, and directed him to bring in profitable returns from the banking business.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 338; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: Callistus is described as a former slave and banker who defrauded Carpophorus and was later punished.
limits: A hostile ad hominem biography. Scholars disagree on how much to trust it. The Greek 'πισχινῇ πουπλιχῇ' is an accepted editorial text (Sauppius suggests 'πισχίνῃ'); read from the image.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium IX.12 (Zephyrinus appoints Callistus over the cemetery; Duncker p. 456) (Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 Greek numbering; ANF vol. 5 ch. 7; ANL vol. 6 p. 341)
greek: Μεθ᾽ οὗ κοίμησιν Ζεφυρῖνος συναράμενον αὐτὸν σχὼν πρὸς τὴν κατάστασιν τοῦ κλήρου, ἐτίμησε τῷ ἰδίῳ κακῷ, καὶ τοῦτον μεταγαγὼν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀνθείου εἰς τὸ κοιμητήριον κατέστησεν.
greek_edition: Duncker-Schneidewin 1859 (Refutationis omnium haeresium librorum decem quae supersunt, Gottingae: Dieterich), Greek text read from 130-dpi render of the Google Books PDF (image only, no text layer); accents as read from the image; editorial brackets kept as printed
english: And after Victor's death, Zephyrinus, having had Callistus as a fellow-worker in the management of his clergy, paid him respect to his own damage; and transferring this person from Antium, appointed him over the cemetery.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5 / ANL vol. 6)
page: ANL vol. 6 p. 341; ANF vol. 5 page unknown
edition: ANL vol. 6, 1868 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.); ANF vol. 5 online text
what_it_says: After Victor's death Zephyrinus brought Callistus back from Antium and set him over the cemetery.
limits: Hippolytus' account. The cemetery is the one Hippolytus names; the Greek 'κοιμητήριον' is the source for the later 'Callistus cemetery' (Via Appia, per the ANL editor's note). Scholarly identification not verified here.
